---
title: "Statistics reference: describe, compare, and interpret"
---

Start with the biological question and the independent experimental unit.
Neither a large table nor a small p-value can repair a design with no
independent replication.

| Quantity | What it describes | Units / interpretation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mean | The arithmetic average of measurements | Same units as the measurement |
| Median | The middle of the sorted measurements | Same units; less affected by a single extreme |
| Sample variance | Squared deviations from the mean, summed and divided by n − 1 | Squared measurement units |
| Sample SD | Square root of the sample variance | Spread among measurements, in their original units |
| Standard error of a mean | Estimated sampling variability of a mean | Common introductory estimate: SD / square root of n for independent observations |
| Confidence interval | Uncertainty in an estimated quantity under a model | A procedure that covers the fixed population quantity in 95% of repeated samples for a 95% interval, when assumptions hold |

An interval around the mean does not describe where 95% of individual plants
will fall. Adding technical repeats of the same plant does not add independent
plants to the sample size.

## The two comparisons taught here

**Independent groups:** separate plants/pots allocated to control and treatment.
Use a guided Welch two-sample t-test for the difference in mean growth. Define
the direction before reporting it, such as treated minus control.

**Paired observations:** the same plant before and after a change. Compute
after minus before within each plant, then analyse the differences. Correctly
matching identifiers is essential; row order in two files is not evidence of
matching pairs.

Both approaches need independent experimental units or pairs. For small samples,
inspect unusual observations and strong skew. A test is conditional on its
assumptions; you are not learning an automatic test-selection algorithm.

A p-value is the probability, under the null model and its assumptions, of a
test statistic at least as extreme as the observed one. It is not the probability
that the null hypothesis is true. Report the estimated difference, its units,
confidence interval, sample sizes, and a biological interpretation. A small
p-value does not establish a large or causal effect; a large one does not
establish equality.

## A straight line

In `lm(y ~ x, data = table)`, the intercept is fitted y at x = 0 and the slope
is the fitted change in y for a one-unit increase in x. The slope's units are
y-units per x-unit. The residual is observed y minus fitted y.

For calibration, standards have known x values; invert the fitted line to obtain
an unknown concentration from its signal, only within a supported range. This
simple calculation provides a point estimate, without full uncertainty
propagation. For an observational biological association, the slope does not
establish what would happen if we intervened to change x.

[week 4](../week4/16-comparisons.qmd) for worked examples.
